The Story of Vishnukumar Muni

I pay homage to the Jina, the Jina's word, and the Jain sages, and write here the story of Vishnukumar Muni, who practiced vatsalya — the limb of right faith that cherishes fraternal love for one's fellow believers.

In the renowned city of Ujjaini, in the land of Avanti, there ruled King Shrivarma. He was righteous, learned in all the scriptures, thoughtful, and brave. He punished the wicked justly and governed his people with wisdom. His queen, Shrimati, was equally learned and compassionate — the people regarded her as a goddess.

But the king had four ministers named Bali, Brihaspati, Prahlad, and Namuchi — all bitter enemies of dharma. A king accompanied by such wicked counsellors was like a sandalwood tree entwined with venomous serpents.

The Acharya's Warning

One day the enlightened Acharya Akampanacharya arrived in Ujjaini with a great assembly of seven hundred monks. Through his power of foresight, the acharya sensed that trouble awaited them in this city. He gathered his monks and warned them: "If the king or anyone else comes to visit, do not engage them in argument. If you do, grave persecution will fall upon the entire community."

The monks honoured their guru's command and sat in silent meditation. Truly, those disciples who follow their teacher's word with love and humility are worthy of praise; those who defy it are like wayward children.

When the citizens learned of the acharya's arrival, they flocked to pay homage with offerings. Seeing the commotion, King Shrivarma asked his ministers what was happening. They replied with contempt, "Naked Jain monks have come to the city, and everyone is running to worship them." The king, being a man of faith, said, "Then we too should go and pay our respects." He found the monks absorbed in meditation and was deeply moved. He bowed to each one in turn, but following the guru's instruction, none spoke a word.

On the way back, the ministers poisoned the king's ear: "Your Majesty, these monks are utter fools — they cannot even speak. Their silence is not meditation but a pretence to deceive the public." And so they sowed seeds of doubt.

The Debate

As they walked, the party encountered a lone monk returning from collecting alms. This monk, Shrutsagar, had been in the city and had not heard the guru's warning. When the ministers mocked him — calling him an ox that had simply filled his belly and walked off — he could not bear the insult. He challenged them to a scriptural debate and defeated them soundly with his learning.

The ministers were humiliated. Their defeat before the king stoked a fury that would soon engulf the entire monastic community.

The Persecution

The wicked ministers devised a cunning plan. They reminded the king of a favour he owed them and demanded the kingdom for seven days. Bound by his word, Shrivarma had no choice but to agree.

With power in their hands, the ministers staged an enormous animal sacrifice. They erected a vast pavilion, placed the monks at its centre, and surrounded them with piles of firewood. Thousands of animals were slaughtered as offerings. The sky darkened with the stench of smoke. It was as though the sun itself set, unwilling to witness such a sin.

But the monks — those embodiments of peace — bore this terrible persecution with unshaken equanimity. They considered it the fruit of their own past karmas and sat immovable as Mount Meru, their minds fixed on the Supreme. Those whose hearts are truly strong, who maintain equanimity towards friend and foe, praise and blame, can never be disturbed by suffering.

The Rescue

Far away in Mithila, Shrutsagar Muni perceived through his clairvoyance what was happening. He cried out in anguish, "A terrible persecution is falling upon seven hundred monks in Ujjaini! Only Vishnukumar Muni can stop it — he has attained the supernatural power called vikriya-riddhi."

The message was carried to Vishnukumar. He had not known of his own power until that moment. Testing it, he stretched out his hand and found it could reach to impossible distances. Confident now, he flew to Ujjaini and confronted his own brother, who held authority in the city. "What catastrophe is unfolding in your realm? The saints of our tradition — peaceful, detached, harming no one — are being persecuted! A king's duty is to protect the righteous and punish the wicked. You are doing the opposite. Even cool water, when heated, can scald the flesh. Put an end to this before it destroys you too!"

Vishnukumar then used his extraordinary powers to extinguish the sacrificial fires, scatter the persecutors, and liberate the suffering monks. The community was saved.

The Teaching

This is the essence of vatsalya: fraternal love that moves one to protect fellow believers in their hour of need. Vishnukumar did not hesitate; he did not calculate the cost. When those bound by faith suffer, the true devotee acts — not out of obligation, but out of love as natural as breathing.
